title: Path Sum
description: Check if a binary tree has a root-to-leaf path summing to a target, using a shrinking-target recursion with early exit.

blocks.text: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return true if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that the sum of the values along the path equals targetSum, otherwise return false. A leaf is a node with no children.

blocks.caption: Subtracting each node's value from a running target as recursion descends turns the check into a simple leaf comparison.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","root (binary tree, may be empty), targetSum"],["Path definition","Root to a leaf (a node with no children)"],["Output","True if any such path sums to targetSum, else false"]]}

blocks.text: Checking every root-to-leaf path against a target is a classic tree recursion (or backtracking) problem: at each node, "carry" the remaining budget (target minus values seen so far) down into the recursive calls, and the check collapses to a simple equality test once a leaf is reached.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Passing a shrinking "remaining target" value down through recursive calls (rather than accumulating a running sum and comparing only at the end) avoids ever needing to track the full path explicitly.

Picture a hiker with a fixed travel budget, descending a tree of trails. At each stop, the cost of that stop is subtracted from the remaining budget. At a dead end (leaf, no further trails), the hike only "succeeds" if the remaining budget is EXACTLY zero relative to that leaf's own cost, meaning the leaf's value exactly matches whatever budget is left before subtracting it.

blocks.caption: A dead end succeeds only if the remaining budget exactly matches that stop's cost.

items: At each node, subtract its value from the remaining target before recursing.
At a leaf, the path succeeds if and only if the leaf's own value equals the remaining target passed into it.
The overall answer is true if EITHER the left or right subtree finds a successful path.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node visited","Remaining target entering this node","Remaining target after subtracting"],"rows":[["5 (root)","22","17"],["4 (left child)","17","13"],["11 (left child)","13","2"],["2 (leaf, left child)","2","leaf value 2 equals remaining target 2, SUCCESS"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The path 5 -> 4 -> 11 -> 2 sums to exactly 22, matching the expected output of true.

A direct approach collects the sum of every root-to-leaf path into a list first, then checks whether the target appears anywhere in that list. This is correct but computes and stores ALL path sums even when an early path already matches.

Passing the shrinking remaining target directly through the recursion, and checking it against each leaf as soon as it is reached, lets the recursion short-circuit the moment ANY matching path is found (via the OR of left and right subtree results), without ever needing to finish exploring the whole tree.
Collect the sum of every root-to-leaf path into a list, then check if the target sum appears in that list.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n)","Every node is visited once to build the sums list"],["Space","O(n)","The list of every leaf's path sum, plus recursion stack"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Computing and storing every single path sum is unnecessary once the recursion can short-circuit the moment any matching path is found.

Pass a shrinking "remaining target" down through the recursion, subtracting each node's value as it descends. At a leaf, check directly whether the leaf's value equals the remaining target. The overall result is the OR of the left and right subtree results, letting the recursion return true as soon as any path succeeds, without exploring the rest of the tree.

items: Base case: an empty tree has no path, so return false.
Leaf case: return whether the leaf's value equals the remaining target.
Otherwise, recurse into both children with (target - current node's value), returning true if either finds a match.

items: Passing a shrinking "remaining target" through a recursion, rather than accumulating a running sum for comparison only at the end, is a memory-efficient technique for path-sum-style tree problems.
Returning the OR of left and right subtree results lets the recursion short-circuit the moment any valid path is found.
This shrinking-budget pattern reapplies to any "does a root-to-leaf path satisfy some additive condition" tree problem.

blocks.text: Path Sum is solved by passing a shrinking remaining target through the tree recursion, subtracting each node's value as it descends, and checking the exact match only at leaves. Returning the OR of both subtrees' results lets the search stop the moment any valid root-to-leaf path is found, using only O(h) extra space for the recursion stack.
